source_text:
ἑτέρως ἢ οὕτως· εἶπε τὴν φύσιν, ὅθεν ἐκ γῆς ἐκ ταύτης καὶ οἱ ἐπουράνιοι καὶ οἱ
λεγόμενοι χοϊκοί· ἀλλ' οὐκέτι χοϊκοὶ ἑκάτεροι. δεῖ τοίνυν προσέχειν ὅτι ὁ μὲν κύριος
ἐξ οὐρανοῦ λέγεται οὐχ οἱ ἐπουράνιοι, οἱ δὲ οὐράνιοι ἀπὸ γῆς οὐχ ὁ ἐξ οὐρανοῦ
κύριος. εἰκόνα χοϊκοῦ λέγει τὴν ἀναστροφὴν τὴν χοϊκήν, εἰκόνα ἐπουρανίου τὴν
ἐπουράνιον πολιτείαν, ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐμιμησάμεθα τὴν παρακοὴν τοῦ Ἀδάμ, μιμησώμεθα
καὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν ὑπακοὴν ὑπακούσαντες. 277 1 Kor 15,50 Κατὰ τῆς
ἀναστάσεως τοῦτο ἕλκουσι πολλοὶ τῶν αἱρετικῶν ὑπὸ πολλῆς ἀνοίας· οὐ γὰρ εἶπεν
ὅτι σὰρξ καὶ αἷμα οὐκ ἀνίσταται, ἀλλὰ βασιλείαν θεοῦ οὐ κληρονομήσει. τῆς
βασιλείας τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀπέκλεισεν, οὐ τῆς ἀναστάσεως τὴν χάριν. ὃ οὖν λέγει
τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν, ὅτι σὰρξ σὰρξ οὖσα οὐ κληρονομεῖ, καὶ αἷμα αἷμα ὂν οὐ κληρονομεῖ·
ἕως γὰρ ἡ σὰρξ σάρξ ἐστι, φθαρτή ἐστιν· λοιπὸν δὲ ἐνδυσαμένη ἀφθαρσίαν τῆς
σαρκὸς ἀποθεμένη τὴν ἀσθένειαν ἕτερόν τι γίνεται, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἄφθαρτον.
Ἀπέδειξεν ὃ ἔλεγεν πρὸ τούτου· ἀφθαρσίαν γὰρ καλεῖ τὴν βασιλείαν, φθορὰν δὲ τὴν
ἐν τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ θνητότητα. τὰ οὖν ἐναντία τῶν ἐναντίων οὐ γίνεται κληρονόμα.
1 Kor 15,52 Ἐδήλωσεν ὅτι πολλαί εἰσι σάλπιγγες· ἐσχάτης γὰρ μνημονεύσας καὶ τὰς
πρώτας συνέθηκεν. Καὶ οἱ νεκροὶ ἐγερθήσονται ἄφθαρτοι, καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα.
εἰ ἄφθαρτοι οἱ νεκροί, καὶ αὐτοὶ ἀλλαγήσονται δηλονότι. τίς χρεία καὶ ἡμεῖς
ἀλλαγησόμεθα; ἢ πάντως που τὸ μὲν ἄφθαρτον κοινὸν εἶπεν πάντων, τὸ δὲ
ἀλλαγησόμεθα τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ κρεῖττον μεταβολὴν αἰνίττεται νῦν· διὸ καὶ ἡμεῖς εἶπε περὶ
τῶν δικαίων. Εἰπὼν τοῦτο καὶ δείξας τὸ σῶμα περιέκλεισε τοὺς αἱρετικοὺς τοὺς
λέγοντας μὴ εἶναι ἀνάστασιν σαρκὸς ἀλλὰ ψυχῆς· οὗτοι γὰρ καὶ περὶ αὐτὴν τὴν
θείαν οἰκονομίαν ἀσεβοῦσιν οἰόμενοι μὴ ἀληθείᾳ ἀλλὰ φαντασίᾳ ἀνειληφέναι τὸν
Χριστὸν τὴν σάρκα, ὅπερ ἀνόητον. εἰ γὰρ σάρκα οὐκ εἶχεν, τί τὸ ἀποθανὸν καὶ ταφὲν
καὶ ἀναστάν; εἰ δὲ φαντασίᾳ ταῦτα, οὐκοῦν καὶ ἡμεῖς φαντασίᾳ ἀποθνῄσκομεν. τὸ
μὲν οὖν ἄφθαρτον κοινὸν τῶν ἐγερθησομένων, τὸ δὲ ἀλλαγῆναι μόνον ἴδιον τῶν
ἁγίων, ὅπερ τὴν ἐπὶ τὸ κρεῖττον μεταβολὴν ἐμφαίνει. τὸ δὲ ἡμεῖς περιττόν, εἰ μή που
βούλεται σημᾶναι περὶ τῶν ἁγίων, ἀντὶ τοῦ οἱ περὶ ἡμᾶς δίκαιοι, ὡς καὶ ἀλλαχοῦ
εἰπὼν ὅτι ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες, τοὺς περὶ αὐτὸν ἁγίους ἐσήμανεν. 1 Kor 16,1 Λογία
λέγεται ἡ κατὰ συλλογὴν γενομένη συνεισφορὰ εἰς παραμυθίαν πενήτων.
pass_a_gloss: [15:47-49 note, continued] ...otherwise than so: he spoke of the nature, whence 'from earth'; from this [earth] both the heavenly ones and those called earthy; but no longer are both earthy. So one must attend that the Lord is said [to be] from heaven, not the heavenly ones, and the heavenly ones from earth, not the Lord from heaven. He calls image of the earthy the earthy conduct, image of the heavenly the heavenly way of life, instead of: we imitated the disobedience of Adam; let us imitate also the obedience of the Son of God by obeying. [Page 277; label 1 Kor 15,50] Many of the heretics, from great folly, drag this against the resurrection; for he did not say that flesh and blood does not rise, but will not inherit the kingdom of God. He shut [them] out of the kingdom of the Son of God, not out of the grace of the resurrection. So what he says is such: that flesh being flesh does not inherit, and blood being blood does not inherit; for as long as the flesh is flesh, it is perishable; but for the rest, having put on incorruption, having put off the weakness of the flesh, it becomes something other, that is, imperishable. He demonstrated what he was saying before this; for he calls the kingdom incorruption, and corruption the mortality in this age. So the opposites do not become heirs of the opposites. [Label 1 Kor 15,52] He made clear that there are many trumpets; for having mentioned the last he put together the first ones too. 'And the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we will be changed.' If the dead are incorruptible, they too clearly will be changed. What need [for] 'and we will be changed'? Or surely he said the incorruptible as common to all, and the 'we will be changed' now hints at the change toward the better; therefore he also said 'we' about the righteous. [Second form] Having said this and having shown the body, he shut in the heretics saying that there is not a resurrection of flesh but of soul; for these are impious even about the divine plan itself, supposing that Christ took the flesh not in truth but in appearance, which is senseless. For if he did not have flesh, what [was] the thing that died and was buried and rose? And if these [were] in appearance, then we too die in appearance. [Not printed again: So the incorruptible is common to those who will be raised, but the being changed is proper only to the saints, which shows the change toward the better.] And the 'we' [is] superfluous, unless perhaps he wishes to signify about the saints, instead of 'the righteous around us', as also elsewhere, having said 'we the living', he signified the saints around him. [Label 1 Kor 16,1] A collection is called the contribution made by gathering, for the comfort of the poor.
pass_b_english: …otherwise than this: he spoke of nature, which is why he says “from the earth.” From the earth come both the heavenly ones and those called earthy, but the two are no longer both earthy. So we must notice that the Lord is said to be “from heaven,” not the heavenly ones, and that the heavenly ones are from the earth, not the Lord from heaven. By “the image of the earthy” he means the earthy way of living, and by “the image of the heavenly” the heavenly way of life. That is: we copied Adam's disobedience; let us also copy the obedience of the Son of God by obeying.

On 1 Corinthians 15:50: Many of the heretics, in their great folly, drag this text against the resurrection. But he did not say that flesh and blood do not rise; he said that they “will not inherit the kingdom of God.” He shut them out of the kingdom of the Son of God, not out of the grace of the resurrection. What he means is this: flesh, while it is flesh, does not inherit, and blood, while it is blood, does not inherit. As long as flesh is flesh, it is perishable; but once it has put on incorruption and laid aside the weakness of the flesh, it becomes something else, that is, imperishable. He has proved what he said before. He calls the kingdom “incorruption,” and “corruption” the mortality of this age. Opposites do not become heirs of their opposites.

On 1 Corinthians 15:52: He made clear that there are many trumpets, for by mentioning the last he implied the first ones too. “And the dead will be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.” If the dead are incorruptible, clearly they too will be changed. What need, then, for “and we shall be changed”? Surely he said “incorruptible” of everyone alike, while “we shall be changed” now hints at the change for the better. That is why he said “we,” of the righteous.

The second catena form adds: By saying this and pointing to the body, he hemmed in the heretics who say there is a resurrection not of the flesh but of the soul. These people are impious even about the divine plan itself, supposing that Christ took flesh not in truth but in appearance, which is senseless. If he had no flesh, what was it that died and was buried and rose? And if these things happened in appearance, then we too die in appearance. The “we” would be superfluous, unless perhaps he means it to point to the saints, standing for “the righteous among us,” just as elsewhere, by saying “we who are alive” (1 Thessalonians 4:17), he pointed to the saints around him.
On 1 Corinthians 16:1: “Collection” is the name for a contribution made by gathering money, for the relief of the poor.
